raw_case_text:
A five-year-old male non-Caucasian patient presented with fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis for 5 days. His past medical history was unremarkable, with normal psychomotor development, no family history neurological diseases and no consanguinity. The patient was born and lived in Ceara, northeast Brazil, and family reported no recent travels.
After 1 week he developed tonic-clonic seizures. Neurological examination was normal at this point. Complete blood count, liver functions and acute reactants were normal. Serologies for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, and toxoplasmosis were negative. Brain MRI was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 15 cells, protein 16.6 mg/dL and glucose 68 mg/dL. He was started on acyclovir and ceftriaxone.
Two weeks after seizure onset, he presented with dystonia (Video 1) and oromandibular dyskinesia. On physical examination the patient was awake, his speech output was decreased, pupils were normal. Cranial nerves examination was unremarkable. Muscle strength was symmetric and deep tendon reflexes were normoactive and symmetric. One week later he developed focal motor seizures followed by decreased level of consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea. EEG showed extreme delta brush and valproate and phenytoin were started. He also received methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulin with seizure resolution and improvement of level of consciousness, dysautonomia and orofacial dyskinesias within 2 weeks.
Anti-NMDAR antibodies were detected in serum (titer 1:25600) and CSF (titer 1:1024) after 3 weeks of symptom onset using tissue and cell-based assays as previously reported. CHIK serology was positive for both IgM and IgG, suggesting a recent infection. Dengue and Zika serologies were negative. CSF PCR for herpes viruses and arboviruses (CHIK, Dengue and Zika) were negative. Whole body CT and testis ultrasound were normal. Because of partial improvement (persistence of orofacial dyskinesias and impaired speech), the patient received rituximab and cyclophosphamide with good response. After 8 months he is seizure-free and has returned to school with only mild restlessness and inattention. Figure 1 describes the timeline of clinical features, investigation and treatment of the case report.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy from Ceara, Brazil, presented with a 5-day history of fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis followed 1 week later by generalized tonic-clonic seizures and subsequent movement disorder and encephalopathy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially developed a 5-day febrile illness characterized by fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis. One week after symptom onset, he developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Two weeks after seizure onset, he presented with dystonia, oromandibular dyskinesia, and decreased speech output, which progressed 1 week later to focal motor seizures, decreased level of consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy non-Caucasian boy born and residing in Ceara, northeast Brazil, with normal psychomotor development, no recent travel, no consanguinity, and no family history of neurological diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, generalized and focal seizures, dystonia, oromandibular dyskinesia, decreased speech, altered consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea.

objective.physical_examination: Initial neurological examination at seizure onset was normal. Two weeks after seizure onset, the patient was awake with decreased speech output, dystonia, and oromandibular dyskinesia, while pupils, cranial nerves, symmetric muscle strength, and normoactive symmetric deep tendon reflexes were preserved. One week later, he exhibited focal motor seizures, decreased level of consciousness, autonomic instability (dysautonomia), and central apnea.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, liver function tests, and acute-phase reactants were normal. Testicular ultrasound was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI and whole-body CT scan were normal. Lumbar puncture cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed mild pleocytosis of 15 cells/mm3, protein 16.6 mg/dL, and glucose 68 mg/dL. Electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrated an extreme delta brush pattern. Autoimmune encephalitis testing at 3 weeks post-symptom onset (using tissue and cell-based assays) was strongly positive for anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) antibodies in both serum (titer 1:25,600) and CSF (titer 1:1,024).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Post-chikungunya autoimmune anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Serum chikungunya virus (CHIKV) IgM and IgG serologies were both positive, indicating recent CHIKV infection, whereas serologies for Zika virus, dengue virus, HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, and toxoplasmosis were negative, and CSF PCR assays for herpesviruses and arboviruses (CHIKV, dengue, and Zika) were negative. He was initially treated empirically with acyclovir and ceftriaxone, followed by antiepileptic therapy (valproate and phenytoin) and first-line immunotherapy with intravenous methylprednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), which resolved his seizures, dysautonomia, and altered consciousness within 2 weeks. Due to persistent orofacial dyskinesias and speech impairment, second-line immunotherapy with rituximab and cyclophosphamide was administered with a good clinical response; at 8-month follow-up, he was seizure-free and had returned to school with only mild restlessness and inattention.
